newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgian ex-president's aide condemned to death.
newsitem.headline: Georgian ex-president's aide condemned to death.

text.p: Supporters of late Georgian president Zviad Gamsakhurdia scuffled with police on Tuesday after the Supreme Court sentenced to death a close associate of the deposed leader.

Loti Kobalia, who led rebel forces in a 1993 civil war when the ousted nationalist Gamsakhurdia tried to retake power from President Eduard Shevardnadze, was found guilty of treason and murder. He and his co-defendants sang in defiance of the judges.
Georgia executes Soviet-style, with a single bullet to the head. But there have been no executions for two years.

Three other Gamsakhurdia associates, including former chief bodyguard Dzhambul Bokuzhava and one-time parliament member Nugzar Molodinashvili, got prison terms ranging from eight to 15 years. Gamsakhurdia himself died in 1993.
Scuffles broke out between police and protesters holding a candlelight vigil outside the court after the sentencing.
Several dozen demonstrators, shouting "Down with Shevardnadze's junta" and waving placards bearing Gamsakhurdia's portrait jostled with police before being dispersed.

Kobalia and his co-defendants, dressed in red Georgian national costume for the reading of the sentence, applauded sarcastically when the death penalty was announced and broke into a rendition of a well-known folk ballad.
Kobalia had pleaded innocent to the charges, which included the execution-style murder during the conflict of journalist Dato Bolkvadze, a cameraman for Worldwide Television News.
Kobalia was found guilty of killing Bolkvadze by pumping bullets into his chest with a Kalashnikov automatic rifle.

Gamsakhurdia, an eccentric nationalist, rode his credentials as a Soviet-era dissident to win Georgia's first presidential election in 1991, as the Soviet Union broke up. He was toppled in January 1992 by opponents who claimed he was a dictator.
A two-week war left the centre of the capital, Tbilisi, in ruins and forced Gamsakhurdia to flee the country.

Former Soviet foreign minister Shevardnadze then returned to lead his native Georgia. Gamsakhurdia launched an uprising aimed at clawing back power after Shevardnadze's army was routed by separatists in the Black Sea region of Abkhazia in 1993.

Kobalia, a former bread-truck driver, led a string of pro- Gamsakhurdia victories before Russian military aid helped save Shevardnadze. Gamsakhurdia died mysteriously that year but his most fanatic supporters believe he is still alive.

Shevardnadze on Monday defended the continued use of the death penalty in Georgia despite international pressure to abandon it. He noted not a single execution has been carried out in two years, though several people are currently on death row.
